title: 06. Memory, State & HITL: Day 12 — Memory & State
summary: Yesterday's agents had no memory. Every .invoke() call started from a blank slate.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Yesterday's agents had no memory. Every `.invoke()` call started from a blank slate. Today you fix that with two complementary techniques:

1. **LangGraph state** — a typed `State` object that persists across turns inside a `StateGraph`. A `MemorySaver` checkpointer snapshots state by `thread_id`, so a user can pause a conversation, come back the next day, and the agent still has the notes it filed.
2. **LangChain message history** — `RunnableWithMessageHistory` automatically appends every user message and AI reply to a `ChatMessageHistory` (in-memory today, Redis or Postgres in production), then re-injects that history into the prompt on the next call.

The first is best when state is structured (notes in categories, partially-filled forms, multi-step plans). The second is best when state is conversational (just remember what we said). Today's projects demonstrate both.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
**Wrong reducer on state fields.** In LangGraph, a field with no `Annotated[..., reducer]` defaults to "overwrite last write wins." If you want a list to accumulate across nodes, you must use `Annotated[List[str], add]`. A common bug is expecting notes to accumulate, forgetting the annotation, then watching your list reset to one item every turn.

**Forgetting to pass `thread_id` in `config`.** The checkpointer keys state by `thread_id`. If you forget to pass `config={"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}` to `graph.invoke`, the checkpointer silently uses a default key and state appears to reset between calls. Always log the thread id at the start of a conversation.

**Mixing up `input_messages_key` and `history_messages_key`.** Both are required by `RunnableWithMessageHistory`. `input_messages_key` tells the wrapper which key in the input dict contains the new user message (so it can append it to history). `history_messages_key` tells it where in the prompt template to inject the loaded history. Mixing them up produces "key not found" errors at runtime.

**History growing unbounded.** `ChatMessageHistory` keeps every message forever. After 50 turns the prompt becomes huge and slow. For production, use `trim_messages` from `langchain_core.messages` to keep only the last N messages, or summarize older turns with a separate LLM call. Day 18 covers this pattern.

**Using `MemorySaver` in production.** `MemorySaver` is in-process and in-memory. It survives within a single Python process but is lost on restart or across workers. For production, use `SqliteSaver`, `PostgresSaver`, or `RedisSaver` from `langgraph.checkpoint.*`. The API is identical — only the import and constructor change.

**State mutation in nodes.** Nodes should never mutate `state` directly — only return a partial dict. Writing `state["notes"].append(...)` inside a node looks like it works (because Python lists are mutable) but the checkpointer may not snapshot the change correctly. Always return `{"notes": [new_item]}` and let the reducer handle it.

sections.title: Next: Day 13 — RAG Agents
sections.body: State and history let agents remember what you said. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets them remember what *you didn't say* — your documents, your Slack history, your wiki. Tomorrow you build a Personal Doc RAG with LangChain + ChromaDB, and a Slack History Searcher with Pydantic AI where retrieval is wrapped as a tool. Both patterns are the foundation of every "chat with your data" product.
